finding.claim: iconUrl is stored without any validation and later fetched by the nightly job, so a caller of PUT /profile can make the server issue GET requests to arbitrary URLs (internal hosts, cloud metadata such as http://169.254.169.254/, localhost services). The response is read into a byte array. The webhook URL, by contrast, is validated.
finding.source: The `icon` parameter of Profile.update(), supplied by the caller of PUT /profile (line 11).
finding.sink: HttpClient.send() with a GET to URI.create(iconUrl) (lines 23-24).

trace.note: update(webhook, icon) receives the attacker-controlled icon from PUT /profile
this.iconUrl = icon stores it with no scheme, host, or IP check
sync() in the nightly job builds a GET to URI.create(iconUrl)
The response body is read with ofByteArray(); the sync() method as written does not return it to the caller

finding.guards_checked: Only webhook is checked, by the full-match regex on line 12. No allowlist, scheme check, or private-IP block applies to icon. The webhook sink on line 21 is not exploitable: String.matches() requires a full match against a fixed host (hooks.example.com) with a 20-character alphanumeric path, and the pattern allows no userinfo, port, or query. The request is a blind or semi-blind SSRF because the response is not returned in this file, but it can still reach internal endpoints.

verdict.reason: src/Profile.java:16 stores the caller-supplied icon unvalidated (only webhook is regex-checked at :12), and sync() at :23 sends a GET to URI.create(iconUrl) with no scheme, host or IP restriction, so this is a blind SSRF.
